messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard deviation (i.e., the standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis is  

\[
\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
=\frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}
\approx 0.2215 .
\]

So the null‑hypothesis test has a standard deviation of roughly **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under null? Usually standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null. That would be sigma/sqrt(n). They gave sample_std_dev=1.4, sample_size=40. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) = 1.4 / 6.3249 = 0.2215 approx.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t distribution is sqrt((n-1)/(n-3))? Actually t distribution has variance (n-1)/(n-3) for n>3. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic? But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." That seems like they want the standard error of the mean difference? Actually the null hypothesis test: H0: mu = 98.6. The test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? Might be the standard error of the mean difference? That is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). So answer: 0.2215.

But maybe they want to compute the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null: same as standard error. So answer: 0.2215.

Alternatively, they might want to compute the standard deviation of the t distribution: sqrt((n-1)/(n-3)) = sqrt(39/37) = sqrt(1.05405) = 1.0268. But that seems less likely.

Given the context, likely they want the standard error. So answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute the p-value using the function. But the user didn't ask for p-value. They asked for standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. So we can compute standard error.

Thus answer: 0.2215.

We can also mention that the standard error is 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.2215. So the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test is about 0.2215.

Thus answer: 0.2215.
